text: A 7-qubit code that beats the Shor code's overhead while keeping the same single-error protection — built directly from a classical code you could study in an undergraduate coding theory class.

The Steane code repurposes the classical Hamming 7,4 code — 7 bits, 4 of them carrying information, able to correct 1 bit error — through its parity-check matrix H, 3 rows by 7 columns. That matrix was directly verified to be self-orthogonal: every one of the 9 pairwise dot products among its 3 rows, including each row with itself, comes out to zero mod 2. That property is exactly the technical condition the CSS construction, next lesson, needs to turn one classical code into a valid quantum code.

Because H is self-orthogonal, the same matrix generates both stabilizer types: 3 X-type stabilizers, one per row — row 1 becomes X4 X5 X6 X7 — and 3 Z-type stabilizers, the same 3 rows with Z instead. That's 6 total generators on 7 physical qubits, encoding 1 logical qubit — the 7-1-3 code, meaning distance 3, correcting any single-qubit error. Self-orthogonality is exactly why this is consistent: an X-stabilizer and Z-stabilizer commute precisely when their rows overlap in an even number of positions, which is what that zero-mod-2 dot product verifies for every pair.

The Shor code needed 9 physical qubits to protect against an arbitrary single-qubit error. The Steane code does the identical job with only 7 — a real, meaningful efficiency gain. And it comes with a bonus the Shor code doesn't have as cleanly: the Steane code's logical Hadamard, X, Z, and CNOT gates can all be applied transversally, qubit by qubit, independently, with no interaction between the 7 physical qubits during the logical gate itself. That property matters enormously for fault tolerance, built out fully in Chapter 7.
Next lesson generalizes what made this construction work — the Calderbank-Shor-Steane, or CSS, recipe — into the dominant family of practical quantum codes.
